title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: A resident challenges Saline Township's tax abatement for a massive hyperscale project, spotlighting power, water and tax shifts statewide.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're leading with a legal challenge to a major tax break for a $43 billion hyperscale data center in Saline Township.
That sounds like it could ripple out to a lot of places. What's the core of this fight?
An attorney is arguing the township skipped required steps when approving the abatement for the Oracle-OpenAI-Related Digital project, and he's asking the state tax commission to deny it.
Why does that procedural step matter so much here?
Because these abatements can shift millions in taxes away from local services like schools and roads, and residents want to make sure the process was followed correctly before that happens.
How big is this project in the bigger picture of Michigan's data center push?
It's one of the largest proposed so far, and it ties directly into the power scramble we're seeing across the state.
Speaking of power, I noticed DTE is looking at a site in Milan Township for a new gas plant to serve these loads.
Exactly. That scouting effort shows how townships far from the main proposals are getting pulled in, and ratepayers 30 miles away could see higher bills if approved.
What about water? These facilities use a lot, right?
They do, and that's why places like Lake Township are writing stricter zoning rules to cap how much water and electricity new centers can draw.
Lake Township is in Huron County, pretty rural. Are residents there worried about their wells?
Yes, the draft rules come as more companies eye Michigan sites, and locals fear strain on the aquifer and the grid.
Manistee Township joined the pause trend today too.
They halted new proposals, aligning with nearby townships and blocking large-scale projects that would draw heavy power and water.
East Lansing extended its moratorium while writing new rules on power use and setbacks.
That gives surrounding townships a model to watch, and it keeps any new proposals on hold until the regulations are set.
How many places are hitting pause now?
It's spreading — Manistee, East Lansing, and others are all taking similar steps to get ahead of the impacts.
What happens if these challenges and pauses keep multiplying?
It could slow the buildout, force more transparent tax deals, and push companies to look elsewhere or negotiate harder on community benefits.
The Lyon Township pushback yesterday was about noise and traffic.
Hundreds of homeowners packed a meeting to oppose a proposed facility they say would add constant hum and truck traffic near homes.
Did officials vote yet?
Not yet — they heard testimony about property values and daily life for people living within a mile.
Detroit suburbs are tightening zoning after similar complaints.
Towns around Detroit are rewriting rules to give local boards more say over size, location and utility demands after residents raised noise, water and grid concerns.
Coldwater has a meeting Monday on power and water strain.
Branch County leaders will hear how new facilities could affect local utility rates and aquifer levels in a joint session with township and county boards.
That sounds like a chance for direct public input before anything advances.
It is — nearby residents get a look at the trade-offs on oversight options.
Back to the Saline challenge — what could the state tax commission do?
They could deny the abatement, which might delay or derail the deal and keep more tax revenue local.
How does this fit the pattern we've seen with other tax fights?
It's the same tension: communities want the jobs and investment but worry about who pays for the infrastructure and lost revenue.
Hyperscale Data sold Bitcoin today to fund its Michigan plans.
The company unloaded 685 BTC, raising cash to slash debt and support its buildout, which could influence future power demand and tax negotiations.
Does that kind of financing detail affect how seriously we take these proposals?
It shows the financial side — companies need liquidity to move fast, but it also means local deals can shift quickly if funding changes.
So the big story here is really about accountability in these deals.
Yes — the legal challenge is testing whether townships are following the rules before handing out big breaks that affect everyone else's taxes.
What should listeners watch for next on this Saline case?
The state tax commission's response, and whether other residents or townships file similar challenges as more projects surface.
It feels like the whole state is figuring this out in real time.
That's why these local fights matter — decisions in one township can set precedents for rates and rules 30 or 60 miles away.
Let's move to some quick hits on the other stories from today.
Manistee Township joined the growing list of places hitting pause on new data centers.
They're blocking large projects that would pull heavy power and water, and residents 30 miles away now face the same uncertainty on growth and rates.
Saline Township's tax break is under legal challenge, as we discussed, which could shift millions away from local services if it stands.
Nearby residents are watching how it plays out for their property taxes and school funding.
DTE is scouting Milan Township for a new gas plant aimed at data-center demand.
That move highlights how the power scramble is pulling in townships across the region, with potential air-quality and rate impacts.
East Lansing kept its data-center freeze in place while staff finish rules on power use and setbacks.
Surrounding townships now have a model to watch for their own zoning fights.
Coldwater officials set a Monday meeting on data-center power and water strain.
Branch County leaders will discuss oversight options with township and county boards before any projects advance.
Lake Township is writing stricter zoning to cap water and power use for new centers.
Rural Huron County residents are concerned about wells and the local grid as more AI server companies look at sites.
Yesterday in Lyon Township, hundreds of homeowners pushed back on noise and traffic from a proposed facility.
They testified it could affect property values and daily life, and the township hasn't voted yet.
Detroit suburbs are also tightening zoning after complaints about noise, water and grid strain.
The changes would give local boards more control, which could protect southeast Michigan ratepayers from higher bills.
Now let's look at what's on deck for listeners who want to attend.
Monday, August 17, Coldwater City Council, Planning Commission and Board of Public Utilities are holding a joint informational meeting on data center impacts, regulation and oversight.
That one pulls in multiple boards so residents can hear directly about utility rates and aquifer levels.
Also on the 17th, Caledonia Township Planning Commission has a data center ordinance discussion and potential zoning amendments.
That's a chance to weigh in on new rules before they lock in.
And Kalamazoo City Commission will vote on a resolution for a temporary moratorium on data center development.
Another pause vote that could set the tone for the area.
Plenty of opportunities for folks to show up and be heard.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.
Thanks for listening — good night.

episode_title: Saline Twp Tax Break for $43B Data Center Faces Legal Fight Over Skipped Steps and Local F
